questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Learning german. I wanted to learn language of the country i would be doing my exchange in. 
I specifically choose Heidelberg over citites like Hamburg and Berlin for its size, surroundings and history. My knowledge about the university came afterwards.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Somewhat easy. Theres always someone you can write an email to. I did feel like I had to doublecheck everything myself tho. Every situation for every exchangestudent is unique.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Lots of informative emails. And then there’s the introweek in the first week of april, but I didn’t really participate. If you take the languagecourse in march, you’ll be able to receive a lot of the same information - also by just living there for over a month before semesterbegin.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Wished they would have informed more about exams, how to recieve the examcertificates etc.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I (somehow?) found it easy. I used WGgesucht, responded to posts on there and got a lot of response. There’s lots of subletting, since many students in Heidelberg are going on exchange themselves, doing internships etc. for a semester or two.
I contacted everyone in german, which i think helped a lot. Fluency is not necessary tho (i wasn’t)! Germans are very open and helpfull when it comes to learning and speaking their language:)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Many of the rooms you can get through studierendenwerk are located in Altstadt - which is nice. But Altstadt is also very small and touristy. Heidelberg isnt that big, so I really recommend looking for housing in some of the other parts:)) Neunheim, Bergheim, Weststadt (!!), Südstadt, but als some of the parts a bit further away form the city center like Handschuhsheim and Rohrbach are adorable

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I registered for everything I found interesting, as I felt very lost in how hard it would be getting the courses I wanted (and also just enough). 
The registration is online, but some of the courses didn’t have the option of registration. Then you’ll just have to write directly to the professors to get registered (which is very normal and also makes it much more personal and charming in my opinion - but is of course a bit more work and feels more unofficial?)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: With the course registration I felt like i was more or less on my own. But as said, theres always someone ypu can write an email too or arrange a physical meeting with. Otherwise just ask the professors directly! Also if you need more information about a specific course:))

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was way more sucessfull than I had expected. I got into every course i had regisered for except one seminar. Since I had registered for more courses than i planned to take, i just deregistered afterwards or just didn’t attend.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Register for everything interesting. 
There’s lots of flexibility, which can be difficult to adapt to/understand coming from KU.. At Heidelberg it’s very normal to shop courses in the first couple of weeks of the semester. Attendance is mandatory, but everything is very much a communication between you and the professor directly, so if you end up not attending a course anyways or want to join a week or two into the semester, it feels like everything can be arranged. The amount of credits you get is dependent on what you personally arrange with your professor at the end of the semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Proseminars are for ba students only. Can be a bit introductory, which I sometimes, as a ba-student on my last semester, found a bit too ‘mild’.
Hauptseminars/Oberseminars are for both ba and ma students. More work, bigger exams and more ects points. 
I only attended proseminars, but in retrospect I would have liked to attend a Hauptseminar too:)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The seminars compares to ‘Holdundervisning’, but with more emphasis on active discussion. Way more intimate (often only around 10 students). In some seminars it is expected that every student do a presentation at some point in the semester. These student-held-presentations makes up 50% of the course, I would say.
Not so much reading, more in depht engagement with a smaller amount of pensum literature.

I really liked Vorlesungen even though it’s also a lot of information and passive listening. Very competent professors!!

Every course (seminar or vorlesung) is 1,5 hour one day a week (unless blockseminar/excursion/something ‘out of the box’)
I felt like i had to put in more work pr ects point in Heidelberg compared to at KU, but i think it’s also because both system and language was new.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
VL Heideggers Baum. Überlegungen zu einer Philosophie des Blicks

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Stephen Westphalens courses on byzantine arthistory and archaology - he is cool:))

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food and alcohol is generally cheaper, so i just ended up buying more…

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: All course literature will be uploaded on the courseplatform (at least the case most of the time) - so literature for uni was way cheaper than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Lots of sportsprograms. Also lots of social events such as movienights or parties where being hosted through the university i think. But i felt like the city lacked events that wasn’t being held within this uni-frame.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go to the theater:)) Its free for the students in Heidelberg. I regret not going there more.. Also the old cinema gloria! Take the S-bahn to Mannheim (15 min) and visit Kunsthalle Mannheim (the museums in Heidelberg are a bit more ://) 
Go an lots of eveningwalks.
If you’re into bouldering, it’s possible to do outside, at Riesenstein, only 15-20 min on foot from Altstadt. It’s also just a nice walk in itself

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Get a bike, bike outside Heidelberg through the countryside. When the rapseedfields bloom!! Bike to Waidsee.
Get the deutschlandticket and leave Heidelberg haha (Frankfurt, Freiburg, i went all the way to Strassbourg with it).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
German culture isn’t that different from danish culture, so not that hard. I think it’s more in the detail, what sets it apart, living there as a student. 
Heidelberg isn’t owerwhelmingly big and is also filled with students, which makes it easier to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The local students are very open!! It’s (somewhat) easy to merge into friendgroups over lunch in the mensa. Just ask if someone wants to grab a coffee - oftentimes the local students themselves don’t know anyone in the specific seminars, since every student follow their own very flexible semesterplans.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The humor? I don’t know… If you get lucky and find the right people, cultural differences and awkwardness (?) can become a way to bond.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Hmm hard to sum up? The academic seriousness? The unexpected social openness? The language and it’s literature?

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Everything is new, so stressfull feelings of uncertainty and inadequacy can become overwhelming. See it as a part of it and just take one thing at a time. Luckily you will be walking around in a fairytale city everyday, so it can never be that bad;) 
Learn the language!! Don’t take yourself too seriously, speak it, you’ll make mistakes (I did everyday) and it doesn’t matter.
Be open<3

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends i made. And honestly learning german, maybe my biggest achievement haha, it opened up the whole experience (wasn’t at all fluent when i came, but things come quickly when you live there if you just dare and try your best).

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Missing the ocean!
The city can feel a bit claustrophobic at times due to it’s size, being surrounded by hills, it’s social homogeneity, being almost too idyllic.. It helps leaving heidelberg for a day, seeing other more diverse parts of Germany.
Homesickness and lonelyness didn’t really take up that much space. Heidelberg is very homely and welcoming almost from day one (at least in the summersemester)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
